items.text: The original source of this table's data (ad_groups) cannot be located anywhere in the Oracle database. The same issue affects several other related tables, including ADJ_CD_DIM, TX_TYPE_DIM, POS_ITEM_TYPE_DIM and OPERATOR_DIM.
A single confirmed process updates this table on a daily schedule, and every row carries the same source label ('HQ') with no exceptions. No other process competes to update this table.
This table has no placeholder 'unknown' row and no duplicate business keys, unlike most other similar tables. It is clean on both counts.

A generic process that creates placeholder rows is technically connected to this table, the same one used for OPERATOR_DIM. Unlike OPERATOR_DIM, where this process created a large share of the rows, here every row is a normal, fully approved record: this process has never actually run against this table.

This table was not part of a group of related tables retired in 2015-2016. Its schedule start date lines up with when it first went live, not with an older process being shut down. Caveat: the file used to check this carries its own warning that it may be incomplete, so this is not full proof the table was never affected by a similar retirement.

The placeholder-creation process file carries a leftover description referring to a different, unrelated table. This is a copy-paste artifact, not a sign that the wrong table is affected: the file's actual behavior confirms it targets AD_GRP_DIM.

The orchestration code explicitly notes that this table's older, dead process was intentionally decommissioned on the same date its staging table went silent, not simply abandoned. A related process for a connected table was found to pull its data from a specific external system named HQAnalytics, and stamps the same source label ('HQ') seen on this table. Neither of this table's own updating processes shows that same explicit connection, so a link to the same external system is plausible but not confirmed.

items.text: Two different loading processes have fed this table over the years. The old one stopped running in 2020 (15,019,410 rows, frozen). The current one runs daily and touched data again this morning (6,958,825 rows)

Serious: the step meant to keep household level benefit flags correct only looks at households that still exist in the staging table frozen since 2020. Any household created or changed since then is silently skipped, its benefit flags never get re-evaluated

Serious, same root cause: the step meant to correct a card's points earning flag also only compares against that same frozen 2020 staging table. For any card active since then, there is no working mechanism left in this table's process to ever fix that flag once it goes wrong

Confirmed: the final step into this table inserts new cards and updates existing ones by matching the internal key. Every update also overwrites the basket discount and points earning flags with whatever the staging table has, which, as found above, is empty from the true source. This is not a hypothesis anymore, it is confirmed in code: any card touched by today's process loses these two settings

Confirmed: the step that copies data from the raw feed into the next staging table always marks every card as approved, and computes a fingerprint used to detect what changed. That fingerprint is built from name, address and contact fields only. A card whose only change is to its discount or points settings would not be picked up as changed at all
26 other tables depend on this one, including the two largest transaction tables in the warehouse. This table has to be migrated before any of them

blocks.text: Still open, not confirmed in code or data yet. None of this blocks the lineage above, it is tracked here so nothing gets forgotten.

items.note: SALES_POS_TX_F, scheduled Wave 2, carries CLUB_CARD_KEY and needs the dimension to exist first.

items.text: The step that fills in a customer's first purchase date has not been fully reviewed yet.
items.note: It is the last unread step in the daily process. Its place in the sequence is confirmed, but whether it has the same frozen-data problem found in the household and points-earning steps is not.

items.text: The process that injects placeholder members from the loyalty points source has not been identified.
items.note: A confirmed placeholder process only handles a different source, the customer survey tool. A separate, still unidentified process must handle the loyalty points source.

items.text: What triggers the process that creates placeholder members from the customer survey tool has not been identified.
items.note: That process has no schedule of its own and is not called by the main daily process, so something else triggers it. Not yet identified.

items.text: Whether a status column is populated only for one particular source system's rows, or the matching counts are a coincidence, has not been confirmed.
items.note: Worth one more check before treating this as a real pattern.

items.text: How many cards already have their basket discount or points earning settings blanked out, versus still showing a real value, has not been measured.
items.note: The cause is now confirmed: every card the daily process touches loses these two settings. A count would show how many cards are already affected.

items.text: The real, observed run schedule for this table's daily process, rather than what its schedule setting states, is still unknown.
items.note: Earlier project notes claim it actually runs twice a day, not once as configured. Not reconfirmed this session.

items.text: The 15,183 stub member figure from references/anomaly-checklist.md has not been reconciled against this session's 240,954.
items.note: This session's number is 16 times higher. Could be growth over time or a different counting basis. Left unresolved rather than asserted either way.

items.text: Important note on validation timing: Row counts for this dimension will not match Oracle during the wave that builds it (Wave 1). The Oracle table contains members inserted by POS_POINTS_EARN_F, migrating in Wave 3, that have not landed yet. This will look like a defect and is not one. Two checkpoints are needed instead of one: a structural checkpoint in Wave 1, confirming columns, keys and transformations, and a row count checkpoint after POS_POINTS_EARN_F lands in Wave 3. Filtering on APPRV_REC_IND separates real members from injected placeholders and makes the first checkpoint meaningful on its own.

A change to the loading process happened on 2025-10-09: the source file name and three cumulative figures (weekly, monthly and year-to-date gallons pumped) stopped being recorded on every row since, including today. Only the daily figures are still populated. Confirmed row by row, not just by matching counts: zero rows in the entire table have one of these fields populated without the others

No formal unique business key is enforced on this table, unlike most tables in this project. A plausible natural combination of columns holds with no duplicates in the data, but nothing in the table's own structure enforces it

This table's two formal links to other tables are both named after a different table name than this one. This strongly suggests the table was renamed at some point and the old links were never renamed with it
One row out of 4.49 million carries an invalid internal key, dated 2018

A related file confirms a named external data connection is used for more than one fuel/loyalty integration in this environment, including a similar report for a different partner program, but that file does not write to this table

items.text: The process that loads this table has not been found anywhere in the available files.

Staging tables exist for center store, pharmacy and fuel counts, all confirmed live. Fresh counts have no staging table under that same naming pattern. A differently named table is a likely but unconfirmed source for fresh counts: its record count, naming and schedule all line up, but no file confirms it actually feeds this table.

Three separate systems feed this table, one for each type of inventory count: PICS for center store and pharmacy counts, STORE_INVENTORY for fresh counts, and VEEDER ROOT (a fuel tank monitoring system) for fuel counts. Each system's record count lines up exactly with its inventory type.
A separate, unrelated fresh inventory process was checked and ruled out as a source: it feeds an item master and pricing catalog for fresh items, not this table.

The documented business key for this table includes a cost figure rather than a purely identifying attribute. This has not been fully checked for duplicates given the table's size; the simpler primary key does hold with no duplicates found.

Which fields are filled in varies by inventory type, and this is a normal business pattern, not a loading gap. Center store counts carry location and retail price detail but not item description or cost. Fresh counts carry item description and cost but almost never a retail price. Pharmacy counts carry item description and cost but not location or retail price. Fuel counts have all of these fields populated.

items.text: This cost table has been rebuilt at least eight times over the years. Only the newest copy is still active and updated this week. The other seven copies have been frozen since late 2019 or early 2020

The true row count is 25.76 billion, measured directly, higher than the database's own quoted statistic of 24.1 billion. Both the measured count and the age of this table, with data going back to November 2019, are extraordinary for a cost table and should be sanity checked with the Weis team before repeating in a client deliverable

One cost adjustment field is populated on only a small fraction of rows, effectively unused across this table's history. A related preferred-vendor field is populated on nearly all rows. The other adjustment fields checked are fully populated
The same pattern repeats one step earlier in the pipeline: six copies of the landing table exist, only one is active

Two sources write this table. One is the running load, HQ, responsible for essentially the entire table and still active today. The other, labelled COST OVERRIDE, touched a small number of rows and has been frozen since May 2023, a one time manual correction rather than an ongoing process

No automatic key assignment happens on insert here, unlike most dimension tables in this warehouse. That is expected: the primary key is a business key (which store, which item, which effective date), not a generated one

blocks.text: Still open, not confirmed in code or data yet. None of this blocks the lineage above, it is tracked here so nothing gets forgotten.

items.text: Which process currently loads this table's staging tables has not been identified yet, despite checking every likely folder for it.
items.note: These staging tables are confirmed live, but the process that fills them has not been found or read. Column naming suggests the same external vendor cost system already seen elsewhere, but the specific process was not located.

items.text: What the two values of the fully populated status field mean has not been confirmed.
items.note: A targeted check or reading the load logic would settle it.

items.text: A second table with the exact same name exists elsewhere in the warehouse, also with 26 columns. Whether it is live, a stale copy, or a duplicate has not been checked. It is excluded from this table's column list and the Data Dictionary until this is resolved, so the dictionary does not show unconfirmed content as if it were verified.
items.note: A direct database check would settle whether this is a leftover copy, frozen like the other duplicate copies, or a real part of the chain.

items.text: About 4 percent of rows are not a clean approved member from the main load. The main load itself creates some placeholder rows, in addition to the three dedicated placeholder sources

One writer source is recorded two different ways in the data, once with an underscore and once with a space in its name. Both are active today. Whether this is one process with inconsistent labeling or two separate processes has not been confirmed
One field, a core POS item flag, is populated on almost all rows but is not produced by either confirmed daily process. Something else maintains it, and that process has not been identified

A recovery version of the nightly process still has a working path to the retired older process, unlike the normal version where that path is disconnected. Whether this recovery path is ever actually used in production has not been confirmed

The daily update process looks up each item's existing identifier by its scan code. When no match is found, it defaults to a known placeholder value, expecting a database mechanism to assign a real value automatically on insert. One row in the live table still carries an unresolved value, so this safeguard does not always work

A shared process that injects placeholder rows across nine dimensions includes a step named for this table. But that step actually writes to a different dimension (location), not this one. This does not explain the placeholder rows measured in this table; that source is still unidentified. The shared process also has no schedule of its own, so whether it runs at all in production is unconfirmed

blocks.text: Still open, not confirmed in code or data yet. None of this blocks the lineage above, it is tracked here so nothing gets forgotten.

items.text: Whether the recovery version of the nightly process, which can still reach a retired older process, is ever actually used has not been confirmed.
items.note: Unlike the normal daily process, where that path is disconnected, this version's path is intact. If it still runs, item identifiers could occasionally be assigned the old, unresolved way.

blocks.text: A few things below are worth knowing before you rely on this table.

items.text: Important note on validation timing: Row counts for this dimension will not match Oracle during the wave that builds it (Wave 1). The Oracle table contains members inserted by SALES_POS_LN_F and VENDOR_ITEM_XREF, both migrating in Wave 2, that have not landed yet. This will look like a defect and is not one. Two checkpoints are needed instead of one: a structural checkpoint in Wave 1, confirming columns, keys and transformations, and a row count checkpoint after SALES_POS_LN_F and VENDOR_ITEM_XREF land in Wave 2. Filtering on APPRV_REC_IND separates real members from injected placeholders and makes the first checkpoint meaningful on its own.

items.text: The obvious staging tables for this data stopped being used in 2016. That does not mean this table itself went inactive: a separate, current process loads it directly from the store master system every day, most recently today.

The current process pulls data directly from 14 distinct tables joined in its own query. Re-checking all 14 against the Oracle catalog directly found that 3 of them are, in fact, real, queryable Oracle tables, not external HQ-side tables as first assumed: STORE_START_END_DATE (documented separately in this catalog), and SALES_AREA / SALES_AREA_ASSIGN (live, 313 and 929 rows, not in this project's scope). The other 11 (store_table, weis_store_status, weis_territory, weis_region, weis_store_hours, the synonym syn_hcd_loc_fuel_open_close, list_detail, lists, pos_areas, weis_county_code, weis_store_department_hours) were individually confirmed absent from every schema this discovery can query, so the true source system for those remains genuinely external and uninspected.

The current process's internal job logging is labeled under a different process's name, apparently copied from another table's loader and never updated. If job monitoring or alerting relies on that name, it is filed incorrectly.

Four columns on this table (legacy banner name, beer cafe open date, beer cafe close date, and pharmacy district number) are no longer updated by the current process. Their values are frozen history and will not change again unless a new process is built to maintain them. A fifth column, marketing cluster, is preserved as-is by the current process but is never assigned a new value.

The current process contains leftover logic for two specific stores that can never actually run, because those two stores are already excluded earlier in the same process. This is leftover code from an earlier version, not an active issue.

All 66 placeholder store records on this table were traced to a handful of supporting processes, most coming from one reusable utility that covers 9 different source tables. One of those processes has a misleading filename (it references a different table) but its own internal target confirms it is meant for this table; it has not actually created any records yet because no matching data exists so far.

blocks.text: Still open, not confirmed in code or data yet. None of this blocks the lineage above, it is tracked here so nothing gets forgotten.

items.text: 11 of the 14 source tables behind this table's daily load are confirmed genuinely external, not visible in any part of the Oracle warehouse this discovery can query: store_table (the main store master source), weis_store_status, weis_territory, weis_region, weis_store_hours, the synonym syn_hcd_loc_fuel_open_close, list_detail, lists, pos_areas, weis_county_code and weis_store_department_hours. The true system behind these has not been identified.
items.note: Knowing what this real source system is, whether a linked database, a separate application, or a manual extract, is necessary before the migration plan can address replacing this feed.

items.text: The process that loads this table appears to run directly on a schedule rather than being called by a wrapper process, breaking the usual pattern seen elsewhere in this project.
items.note: Worth confirming directly against the scheduling system, since the same pattern break was already seen on another table.

items.text: Three differently named versions of the process that manages placeholder store creation exist, and it has not been determined which one is actually in current use.
items.note: This does not block understanding this table, since the individual pieces are already confirmed active from the data, but it will matter for any future table analysis that depends on this specific process.

blocks.text: A few things below are worth knowing before you rely on this table.

items.text: Important note on validation timing: Row counts for this dimension will not match Oracle during the wave that builds it (Wave 1). The Oracle table contains members inserted by SALES_DAILY_BUDGET_F, SALES_POS_TX_F and VENDOR_LOC_XREF, all migrating in Wave 2, that have not landed yet. This will look like a defect and is not one. Two checkpoints are needed instead of one: a structural checkpoint in Wave 1, confirming columns, keys and transformations, and a row count checkpoint after SALES_DAILY_BUDGET_F, SALES_POS_TX_F and VENDOR_LOC_XREF land in Wave 2. Filtering on APPRV_REC_IND separates real members from injected placeholders and makes the first checkpoint meaningful on its own.

New rows are only added, never changed. What triggers the staging step, and which of its several versions is the one actually used, has not been confirmed.

A separate, older set of processes was reviewed and confirmed unrelated to this table. It targets a different table that no longer exists in this Oracle system today, and never references this table by name.

Both this table and its staging area are confirmed active, with data as recent as the last day. Data comes from two distinct sources: the main HQAnalytics receiving feed, and the smaller, unidentified 'shipper content' source described above.

items.text: The daily incremental update process contains a coding flaw: when a genuinely new record has no existing match, it is assigned a fixed placeholder value instead of a proper new key. If more than one truly new record appeared in the same run, they would incorrectly overwrite each other under that same placeholder value.
The full reload process resets the original creation date on every row each time it runs, overwriting the true history of when each record was first created.
The process that loads this table can be triggered from two separate schedules. Whether this causes the load to run twice has not been confirmed.

One of the five columns that make up this table's business key is missing a formal link to its reference table, unlike the other four. Whether this actually causes invalid values has not been measured, since checking it directly would require an expensive scan across two very large tables.
This table has a single confirmed source, marked 'HQ' throughout. It is live, with data as recent as 2026-09-03.

The full loading chain for this table is confirmed. Data arrives daily from the HQAnalytics system, is staged, matched against price level, price type, store and date reference data, and then either updated incrementally or fully reloaded.

items.text: About 74% of this table (1,615 of 2,194 rows) is placeholder data automatically generated by another process, not real operator records, and new placeholders are still being added today. The process that should load real operator records stopped working over 10 years ago (2016), despite being scheduled to run every day

Closer checking shows the suspected source does not fully hold up: the placeholder-creating process has a built-in default source (a POS sales transaction table) that produces a different result than what actually appears on the placeholder records, meaning some other process must be supplying the real source before it runs. This also shows the same shared template is separately used elsewhere against POS transaction data, for an unrelated purpose
The process that creates these placeholder records is a shared, reusable template used across several tables. The specific source it draws from for this table has not been identified

The likely real source of these placeholder records is WMBI.OVERRIDES_ALERTS_F (17,746,540 rows, live), based on a naming and column match. This has not been confirmed by any process explicitly linking the two tables
The source system for real operator records, eamtran_operator_dim, cannot be located anywhere in the Oracle environment, the same issue already found on the TX_TYPE_DIM and POS_ITEM_TYPE_DIM tables
Unlike every other lookup table reviewed so far in this project, this table has no generic 'unknown' placeholder row

3 unrelated files carry a leftover header comment claiming to affect this table, but their actual content is unrelated general ledger work with nothing touching this table: a mislabeled template comment, the same pattern already seen elsewhere in this project
A duplicate staging table exists alongside the live one but holds no data and has never been used: a dead, unused copy, not a second active pipeline

items.text: The tables originally expected to feed this dimension are empty and unused. That did not mean the dimension itself is dead: a different process loads it directly from HQ's store department and accounting systems, with no intermediate staging step, and updates it daily, most recently today. This is the same pattern already found on the location dimension (LOC_DIM): same author, same scheduling style, same direct-load-from-HQ approach. Confirmed by directly checking: neither source table exists anywhere in this Oracle environment, under any schema or object type.

The live loading process's own internal activity logging is mislabeled under a different process's name, not its own. The identical mistake was already found on the location dimension's loader, which logged under yet another process's name. This looks like a repeated copy-paste habit across this author's direct-load files, not an isolated mistake.

6 of the 101 department rows are unapproved placeholders, not real departments, and all have been frozen since 2014-2015, never touched again. The current live loader is not responsible for them: it always marks new rows as approved when its own source data is missing. Two utility processes exist that could in theory create this kind of placeholder, but neither can be tied to these specific 6 rows, and one of them is flagged as broken. Where these 6 rows actually came from is unconfirmed. This matters because one of them, department code '000', is behind 2,678,364 sales records, not a trivial edge case.

A second, undocumented table (PROD_POS_DEPT_DIM) exists with the exact same structure as this one. Its earliest record matches this table's earliest record down to a fraction of a second, strongly suggesting it is a copy taken at some point. It has not been touched since 2019, and nothing in the available material explains its purpose.

blocks.text: Still open, not confirmed in code or data yet. None of this blocks the lineage above, it is tracked here so nothing gets forgotten.

items.text: The purpose and origin of the second, undocumented table (PROD_POS_DEPT_DIM) are unknown, despite its structure and earliest record matching this table exactly.
items.note: If this is a genuine backup or an old copy, it likely does not need migrating. If it is a second table still in active use elsewhere, that changes the migration plan. Ask the Weis team directly what this table is.

items.text: The process that loads this table daily has no clear owning process or caller identified anywhere in the available material, the same gap already seen on the location dimension and another table.
items.note: Worth confirming with the Weis team, via the scheduler that actually runs these jobs, that this process genuinely runs on its own.

items.text: The 6 frozen 2014-2015 unapproved department rows cannot be traced to any known process, and one of them (department code '000') is behind 2,678,364 sales records.
items.note: Not a low-priority detail: a meaningful volume of sales data resolves to an unapproved, undescribed department. Worth asking Weis directly what department code '000' represents and whether it should be a real, approved department.

Two separate processes target this table, the same pattern already found on TX_TYPE_DIM: one runs daily and reads from a source that does not resolve in this Oracle environment, and the other was a one-time 2013 setup. Neither is directly confirmed as the one producing today's data
The source system for the likely real writer, eamtran_item_type, cannot be found anywhere in the Oracle environment, the same issue already found on TX_TYPE_DIM's own source table

The one-time 2013 setup process is called through more than one route in the available material, including a dedicated wrapper found later in the review, but none of these routes has an identified owner or schedule of its own. All of them lead into the same historical, now-dead process, not a separate live one
No placeholder rows exist across all 13 rows, meaning the confirmed placeholder-creating process (fed from sales line data) has never had to add a new item type since at least 2017

items.text: The loader's own source is an older-style file-based master, not a direct database connection, and does not declare where its underlying data actually lives. This is the same unresolved-source pattern already found on several other lookup tables in this project
A single process loads this table daily and accounts for 39 of its 40 rows, matching all current data exactly. No competing process exists

The table has not been touched in about 5 years, longer than the freeze period seen on two similar reference tables in this project (about 2 and 2.5 months). On a table this small (40 rows, a fixed list of pricing methods), this is plausibly just a stable reference list rather than evidence the job itself has stopped; not confirmed either way
One deliberate default row exists for unmatched cases, using a different 'unknown member' convention than the pattern used on most other lookup tables in this project
A shared placeholder-creating utility, also used by AD_GRP_DIM and OPERATOR_DIM, is confirmed to target this table, but has never actually fired here: all rows remain approved

This table was not part of the 2015-2016 wave of table retirements documented elsewhere in this project. That documentation itself carries a warning that it may be incomplete, so this absence is a weaker signal than a positive match would be; it does not prove this table was never part of a similar retirement

items.text: New reclamation scan data has not been added since roughly April 25-26, 2026, more than four months before this analysis. The staging tables looked current on paper, but that was misleading: the underlying scan dates themselves had not moved past that same window, meaning the most recent refresh most likely reloaded the same old data rather than adding anything new

The feed's own schedule shows no sign of being turned off, yet the actual reclamation scan data stopped updating around April 25-26, 2026. If this is indeed the feed that loads this table, the schedule staying active while the data stalled points to a silent failure somewhere upstream, not a deliberate shutdown

All rows in this table come from a single feed, IRC, which matches a real, still-scheduled data integration that has run daily since 2020. That integration calls out to an external system. A related feed confirms IRC-branded integrations pull from a real database on the HQ side, which supports that this is a genuine, active feed, though it is not yet confirmed that this specific integration is the one loading this table
No duplicate or invalid key values were found across all 48.9 million rows, based on the primary key check performed

A later file export supplies the pre-staging loader's own column layout, which marks this field MISSING=ON, but 18 of the file's other 23 columns carry the same flag: a blanket tolerance on this error-capture descriptor, not a signal specific to CARD_TYPE. It does not explain why CARD_TYPE is the one blank on every single row

A related file was found that extracts data from a similar source, a Sunoco location report, into a plain export file rather than into this table. Its columns closely match this table's own columns, which suggests the same underlying source likely feeds this table, but that is not confirmed

'EME', the name identifying the system that writes to this table, is not explained anywhere in the available records. The same name identifies the writer of the Club Card dimension table as well, and is confirmed live and current on both tables

items.text: This vendor-item crosswalk is written by four sources. The main load, from Weis's HQ vendor system, accounts for just over 1 million rows, all of them valid, confirmed entries, none of them placeholders. Two other sources insert placeholder entries when a downstream process could not find a match: about 10,264 rows combined. A fourth source, a single row from March 2019, has never run again
About 1 percent of rows, 10,264 of them, are placeholders rather than confirmed entries. The main HQ load does not create any of these itself; every row it writes is already a confirmed, valid entry

The two least-used vendor and manufacturer code fields are legitimately sparse, not missing data. Their actual population matches expectations closely: about one in five rows carries a manufacturer item code, about one in nine carries a vendor's own item code

This table's staging pattern is the reverse of the item dimension's. Its initial landing table is the active one, touched this week; a later-stage staging table has been frozen since August 2021. This is resolved: the active loading process does not use that frozen table at all, it builds this table directly from the landing table, matched against the item, vendor and warehouse supplier lists

This table's loading process would silently skip a row that could not first be matched to the item, vendor or warehouse supplier lists. That risk is avoided because the same daily run first adds a placeholder entry to any of those lists that is missing one, before the load runs

This table uses the same temporary placeholder-numbering convention seen elsewhere in this project: a record with no existing match gets a stand-in value until the table's own numbering system assigns it a permanent one on insert

items.text: The process that loads this table is not included in the available files. A thorough search turned up only one unrelated mention, a placeholder template built for a different table that happens to reference this table's staging area by default. It does not identify who actually writes to this table

Both this table and its staging area are confirmed active, refreshed as recently as today. A sample of the most recent data shows it comes from two distinct sources, a warehouse shipments feed and a process labeled 'Shipper Content Pass'. This is a gap in the available files, not evidence the loading process does not exist: the same situation was found on the customer segment table, but that table had been inactive for seven years, while this one is actively live

This is directly relevant to an open question on the warehouse supplier list: that table's safety-net process shows a few unresolved records pointing back to this table's staging area, implying something overrides its default settings to read from here. This table's staging area being confirmed active supports that such a process genuinely exists in production, but its code is absent from the available files, just like this table's own loader, so it remains unidentified

Unlike every other reference table reviewed so far in this project, this table's automatic key-numbering feature is turned off. Whatever process writes to this table must supply its own record key directly, rather than relying on the database to assign one

In a sample of the most recent data (79,644 rows), no invalid supplier, location, item or department codes were found. This is not a guarantee across the full table, which holds 755.7 million rows; a complete scan was not run

A closer look at the wording stored on the still-unresolved placeholder rows shows the confirmed caller above does not actually explain them. The 3 rows still awaiting approval reference a different table, WAREHOUSE_SHIPT_F (warehouse shipments), as their origin. No process calling the safety net with that reference was found in the available files; it is likely part of that table's own loading process, not yet analyzed. Separately, the other 51 rows that were already resolved had their names overwritten with real company names by the daily update, so it can no longer be determined from the data alone which process originally created those

This table has a single confirmed process updating it daily since 2017. It always marks every row it touches as approved and from the same source, matching 7,953 of the table's 8,008 rows exactly. No competing process writes to this table's key fields directly, though an older, unused staging table exists with no confirmed reader

A safety-net process that adds placeholder supplier records is confirmed to feed this table. Unlike similar cases elsewhere in this project, its actual caller was found: it is part of the vendor-item crosswalk's own update process, which looks up unresolved supplier codes and adds a placeholder when needed. This confirms that another warehouse process genuinely does insert reference records into this table, a pattern already documented elsewhere in this project
No generic 'unknown supplier' placeholder row exists on this table, unlike most other reference tables reviewed so far in this project, and no duplicate supplier codes were found

This table was not part of the 2015-2016 wave of deliberate shutdowns documented for several other reference tables in this project; no such note exists for it in that record. This is an absence-based conclusion, which carries less weight than a positive confirmation would

One confirmed source of inserted members, VENDOR_ITEM_XREF, also migrates in Wave 2 but later in the wave; a second, unconfirmed source appears to trace to WAREHOUSE_SHIPT_F, which does not migrate until Wave 4. This will look like a defect and is not one. Two checkpoints are needed instead of one: a structural checkpoint early in Wave 2, confirming columns, keys and transformations, and a row count checkpoint after VENDOR_ITEM_XREF lands later in Wave 2, revisited again once WAREHOUSE_SHIPT_F lands in Wave 4 if the second source is confirmed. Filtering on APPRV_REC_IND separates real members from injected placeholders and makes the first checkpoint meaningful on its own.
